newsitem.title: USA: SEC chairman creates investment adviser task force.
newsitem.headline: SEC chairman creates investment adviser task force.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt on Friday announced the creation of a special task force aimed at improving how the financial industry watchdog regulates investment advisers.
"We are redoubling our efforts to make sure that our rules and interpretations protect the millions of investors who today rely on investment advisers," Wall Street's top regulator said.
The agency's actions follow Congress's enactment last year of legislation splitting regulatory jurisdication over advisers between the SEC and states. The agency has proposed similar regulations.
The law authorises the SEC to regulate advisers with more than $25 million in assets under management. States would have jurisidiction over advisers managing less assets.
Levitt said the legislation provides a good starting point for taking a "fresh look" at the agency's rules and "clean out any cobwebs that may have grown over the years."
The 18-month task force will be headed by Robert Plaze, an associate director in the agency's investment management division, and will be staffed with eight lawyers.
After the initial 18-month period, the panel will become a permanent part of the agency's Investment Management division.

The task force will be responsible for putting into effect recent legislation, overseeing SEC participation in an electronic filing system for investment advisers and developing a system enabling investors to obtain information on investment advisers.
The new panel also will review existing SEC regulations and help bring them up to date in light of developments in the marketplace and the investment adviser industry.
In December, the agency proposed investment adviser rules, but the proposal was criticised by the Government Finance Officers Association, a state and local government group.
The association said the agency's plan went beyond Congress's intent and would violate the Constitution by stripping states of their power to adequately regulate investment advisers.
